# Thread Builders

Thread builders, introduced in Java 21 as part of
[JEP 444: Virtual Threads](https://openjdk.org/jeps/444), configure individual
threads or reusable `ThreadFactory` instances. This example configures platform
and virtual threads directly, then creates a virtual-thread factory whose
workers are named `Virtual worker-0`, `Virtual worker-1`, and so on.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- configure a platform or virtual thread with a name and an uncaught-exception
  handler before starting it;
- create a reusable `ThreadFactory` from a thread builder and explain how its
  naming counter is applied; and
- explain why virtual threads must be awaited explicitly when their work must
  finish before the JVM exits.

## Prerequisite

Install an
[Oracle Java 21](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java21)
JDK or newer and ensure `java` and `javac` resolve to it in the terminal.

## The program to inspect

### Configuring and starting individual threads

`Thread.ofPlatform()` and `Thread.ofVirtual()` each return a builder. The
example configures a name and an uncaught-exception handler on each builder,
then calls `start` to create and start the thread. Both thread bodies
deliberately throw an `IllegalStateException`, so their configured handlers make
the per-thread configuration observable. The main thread waits for both threads
to terminate before starting the `ThreadFactory` example.

```java
final Thread platformThread = Thread.ofPlatform()
        .name("Platform Thread")
        .uncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, exception) -> logError("The exception escaped platform thread: " + thread + "!!", exception))
        .start(Main::throwExpectedException);

final Thread virtualThread = Thread.ofVirtual()
        .name("Virtual Thread")
        .uncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, exception) -> logError("The exception escaped virtual thread: " + thread + "!!", exception))
        .start(Main::throwExpectedException);

/* Virtual threads are always daemon threads, so they do not keep the
    JVM alive. There is no public API to make a virtual thread
    non-daemon. If it must complete before the JVM exits, wait for it
    explicitly, for example by calling join(). */
waitForAllThreadsToComplete(platformThread, virtualThread);

logSection("ThreadFactory example");
ThreadFactoryExample.run();
```

### Creating a reusable thread factory

A builder can also create a reusable `ThreadFactory`. This example uses a
virtual-thread builder to create a factory whose workers are named
`Virtual worker-0`, `Virtual worker-1`, and so on. The factory owns the counter,
so each worker has a distinct name without manual bookkeeping. The workers are
started explicitly and the example waits for both to complete.

```java
final ThreadFactory workers = Thread.ofVirtual()
        .name("Virtual worker-", 0)
        .factory();

final Thread firstWorker = workers.newThread(ThreadFactoryExample::runTask);
final Thread secondWorker = workers.newThread(ThreadFactoryExample::runTask);
firstWorker.start();
secondWorker.start();
```

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from this example directory. Choose one of the following ways
to run the example.

1. Run the example using the
   [Maven `exec` plugin](https://www.mojohaus.org/exec-maven-plugin/).

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean compile exec:exec
   ```

2. Build the application and create the JAR file.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) List the created JAR file.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name './target/libs'
   ```

   The application JAR file

   ```
   ./target/libs
   └── thread-builders-1.0.0.jar

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

   Run the application.

   ```shell
   java \
     --module-path './target/libs' \
     --module demo
   ```
